claim: Microtubules in Drosophila oocytes are nucleated or anchored at the cortex and grow from the membrane into the volume.
source: MTs in the oocyte are nucleated or anchored at the cortex (Theurkauf et al., 1992; Parton et al., 2011) and grow from the membrane into the volume.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work (Theurkauf et al., 1992; Parton et al., 2011).

claim: The cortical MT density follows a steep gradient along the posterior-lateral cortex from high density at the anterior corners to low densities at the posterior pole.
source: The cortical MT density follows a steep gradient along the posterior-lateral cortex from high density at the anterior corners to low densities at the posterior pole (Figure 1D, 'Materials and methods' MT nucleation probability).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and described in the methods section.

claim: The model computed more than 55,000 MTs for each realisation of a 3D wild-type cytoskeleton.
source: In total, we computed more than 55,000 MTs for each realisation of a 3D wild-type cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the computational model parameters used in the study.

claim: The computed MT meshwork cross section bears a striking resemblance to confocal images of Tau- and EB-1-tagged MTs.
source: A cross section through the computed MT meshwork (Figure 1A,B) bears a striking resemblance to confocal images of Tau- (Micklem et al., 1997; Ganguly et al., 2012) and EB-1- (Parton et al., 2011) tagged MTs, correctly showing the pronounced AP gradient of MT density.
evidence: The claim compares computational results (Figure 1A,B) with experimental observations cited from previous studies.

claim: The model reproduces the experimentally measured directional bias with 8.5% more MT segments pointing posteriorly than anteriorly.
source: Taking into account the orientations of all MT segments in the 3D volume, it also reproduces the experimentally measured directional bias (Parton et al., 2011) with 8.5% more MT segments pointing posteriorly than anteriorly (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with experimental measurements (Parton et al., 2011) and computational results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The directional bias in a 2D slice varies depending on the depth of the slice in the oocyte, ranging from 50.7% of posteriorly oriented MT segments at the cortex to 60.6% in the mid plane.
source: The directional bias in a 2D slice varies depending on the depth of the slice in the oocyte, ranging from 50.7% of posteriorly oriented MT segments at the cortex to 60.6% in the mid plane (Figure 1B, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational data shown in Figure 1B inset.

claim: Measurements in 2D confocal slices poorly characterise the fully extended 3D system.
source: This demonstrates that measurements in 2D confocal slices poorly characterise the fully extended 3D system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that directional bias varies with depth.

claim: MTs disappear after 5–10 min in the presence of Colchicine.
source: MTs disappear after 5–10 min in the presence of Colchicine (Theurkauf et al., 1992; Zhao et al., 2012) (V Trovisco, personal communication), a drug that blocks MT growth and destabilizes dynamic MTs, indicating that the whole network turns over within minutes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies and personal communication.

claim: The whole MT network turns over within minutes.
source: MTs disappear after 5–10 min in the presence of Colchicine (Theurkauf et al., 1992; Zhao et al., 2012) (V Trovisco, personal communication), a drug that blocks MT growth and destabilizes dynamic MTs, indicating that the whole network turns over within minutes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Colchicine experiment results.

claim: The oocyte samples many tens to a hundred of independent MT organisations over the 6–9 hr of stage 9.
source: Thus, the oocyte samples many tens to a hundred of independent MT organisations over the 6–9 hr of stage 9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MT turnover time and the duration of stage 9.

claim: Summation of local orientations over an ensemble of 50 independent realisations of the computed MT network reveals a striking spatial partitioning of the cytoskeleton into several subcompartments.
source: Summation of local orientations over an ensemble of 50 independent realisations of the computed MT network reveals a striking spatial partitioning of the cytoskeleton into several subcompartments (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational results shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At the anterior, the mean orientation points posteriorly, while MTs at the lateral sides on average point inwards toward the AP-axis.
source: At the anterior, the mean orientation points posteriorly, while MTs at the lateral sides on average point inwards toward the AP-axis.
evidence: This is a description of the computational results from the ensemble average.

claim: The MT density exhibits a pronounced AP gradient with highest values in the anterior corners, even when MT seeding is uniform on the anterior surface.
source: Counting the number of MT segments that contribute to each grid box in the ensemble also shows the distribution of MT density (Figure 1H). In agreement with experiments (Figure 1D), the MT density exhibits a pronounced AP gradient with highest values in the anterior corners, even when MT seeding is uniform on the anterior surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational results (Figure 1H) and comparison with experimental data (Figure 1D).

claim: The mean topology of the MT cytoskeleton is insensitive to the exact choice of the MT nucleation probability and to the choice of the MT length distribution.
source: This mean topology of the MT cytoskeleton is insensitive to the exact choice of the MT nucleation probability and to the choice of the MT length distribution ('Materials and methods' MT nucleation probability, MT growth).
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the model results based on testing different parameters.

claim: The mean topology remains unchanged in a differently shaped oocyte geometry in both the polymer model and the rod model.
source: It also remains unchanged in a differently shaped oocyte geometry in both the polymer model and the rod model (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even disordered non-centrosomal MT arrays can feature well-defined mean organisations.
source: In summary, both models show that even disordered non-centrosomal MT arrays can feature well-defined mean organisations, and that the MT cytoskeleton in oocytes is organised in a compartmental fashion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: The MT cytoskeleton in oocytes is organised in a compartmental fashion.
source: In summary, both models show that even disordered non-centrosomal MT arrays can feature well-defined mean organisations, and that the MT cytoskeleton in oocytes is organised in a compartmental fashion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: During stage 9, the oocyte cytoplasm undergoes slow cytoplasmic flows that are abolished in kinesin heavy chain mutants.
source: In vivo during stage 9, the oocyte cytoplasm undergoes slow cytoplasmic flows that are abolished in kinesin heavy chain mutants.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental observations in wild-type and mutant oocytes.

claim: Flows are driven by kinesin-dependent transport of an unknown cargo through the viscous cytoplasm.
source: This indicates that flows are driven by kinesin-dependent transport of an unknown cargo through the viscous cytoplasm (Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Serbus et al., 2005), thus making cytoplasmic flows a secondary read-out of cytoskeletal organisation (Khuc Trong et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Cytoplasmic flows are a secondary read-out of cytoskeletal organisation.
source: This indicates that flows are driven by kinesin-dependent transport of an unknown cargo through the viscous cytoplasm (Palacios and St Johnston, 2002; Serbus et al., 2005), thus making cytoplasmic flows a secondary read-out of cytoskeletal organisation (Khuc Trong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that flows depend on kinesin activity, supported by citations.

claim: Mean flow velocities in stage 9 oocytes are slow.
source: Measurements of speeds of autofluorescent yolk granules in live stage 9 oocytes showed that mean flow velocities are slow (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Computed and in vivo flows show very similar patterns, generally being strongest in the anterior half of the oocyte, and weaker in the posterior half.
source: Despite large variability, both computed and in vivo flows show very similar patterns, generally being strongest in the anterior half of the oocyte, and weaker in the posterior half (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim compares computational results (Figure 2B) with experimental observations (Figure 2C).

claim: Computed flows occasionally reach further into the posterior half than typically seen in PIV flow fields, thereby slightly overestimating the range of flows.
source: Computed flows occasionally reach further into the posterior half than typically seen in PIV flow fields, thereby slightly overestimating the range of flows.
evidence: This is an observation comparing computational results with experimental data.

claim: Except in rare cases, computed flows do not reach the posterior pole.
source: However, except in rare cases, computed flows do not reach the posterior pole.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational results.

claim: The oocyte nucleus occupies less than 2.5% of the oocyte volume, even for small oocytes at the beginning of stage 9.
source: This result is largely independent of the presence of the oocyte nucleus which occupies less than 2.5% of the oocyte volume, even for small oocytes at the beginning of stage 9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, 'Materials and methods' Nucleus to oocyte volume ratio, Impact on flow field).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and described in the methods.

claim: Computed flows appear consistent with observed slow cytoplasmic streaming.
source: Thus, computed flows appear consistent with observed slow cytoplasmic streaming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing computational results with experimental observations.

claim: Kinesin moves only 13% of oskar mRNA at any given time.
source: Kinesin moves only 13% of oskar mRNA at any given time, and the remaining 87% is subject to diffusion and slow cytoplasmic flows that are driven indirectly by Kinesin activity on the MT network (Zimyanin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work (Zimyanin et al., 2008).

claim: The remaining 87% of oskar mRNA is subject to diffusion and slow cytoplasmic flows that are driven indirectly by Kinesin activity on the MT network.
source: Kinesin moves only 13% of oskar mRNA at any given time, and the remaining 87% is subject to diffusion and slow cytoplasmic flows that are driven indirectly by Kinesin activity on the MT network (Zimyanin et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work (Zimyanin et al., 2008).

claim: Starting from an initial diffuse cloud of oskar mRNA in the centre of the oocyte, simulations show that the mRNA quickly concentrates in the centre before forming a channel from the centre of the oocyte towards the posterior pole.
source: Starting from an initial diffuse cloud of oskar mRNA in the centre of the oocyte (Figure 3A,D,E), simulations show that the mRNA quickly concentrates in the centre before forming a channel from the centre of the oocyte towards the posterior pole (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Formation of the oskar mRNA channel reflects the locally inwards orientation of MTs in the posterior half of the oocyte.
source: Formation of this channel reflects the locally inwards orientation of MTs in the posterior half of the oocyte (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the simulation results to the MT organization shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The transient channel state closely resembles transient patterns of fluorescently-tagged oskar mRNA during the transition between stages 8 and 9.
source: This transient state closely resembles transient patterns of fluorescently-tagged oskar mRNA during the transition between stages 8 and 9 (Figure 3B), thereby supporting the notion that our computed MT cytoskeleton correctly captures key aspects of the in vivo MT network.
evidence: The claim compares simulation results with experimental observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: oskar mRNA localises normally at stage 9 when anchoring is disrupted.
source: However, oskar mRNA localises normally at stage 9 when anchoring is disrupted (Micklem et al., 2000; Vanzo and Ephrussi, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Anchoring is not necessary at stage 9.
source: Anchoring is therefore not necessary at stage 9, and we did not include it in our model at this point.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that oskar mRNA localises normally without anchoring.

claim: Despite the lack of any anchoring, oskar mRNA forms a posterior crescent after 1.5 hr and becomes highly concentrated by the end of the simulation.
source: Despite the lack of any anchoring, oskar mRNA forms a posterior crescent after 1.5 hr and becomes highly concentrated by the end of the simulation (Figure 3F), correctly capturing observations of in vivo localisation (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results (Figure 3F) and comparison with experimental observations (Figure 3C).

claim: A 4 μm thick slice at the posterior pole contains 12.5% of total cargo in the oocyte.
source: A 4 μm thick slice at the posterior pole contains 12.5% of total cargo in the oocyte (Figure 3F), showing that continual transport combined with slow diffusion is sufficient to reach and maintain high concentrations of mRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Continual transport combined with slow diffusion is sufficient to reach and maintain high concentrations of mRNA.
source: A 4 μm thick slice at the posterior pole contains 12.5% of total cargo in the oocyte (Figure 3F), showing that continual transport combined with slow diffusion is sufficient to reach and maintain high concentrations of mRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: In the absence of cytoplasmic flows, oskar mRNA still localises to and forms a concentrated crescent at the posterior pole.
source: We first tested localisation in the absence of cytoplasmic flows by setting the fluid flow field identical to zero u ≡ 0. This situation is similar to but more severe than in slow Kinesin mutants (Serbus et al., 2005). Starting from the central oskar mRNA cloud (Figure 3D), we found that oskar mRNA still localises to and forms a concentrated crescent at the posterior pole (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A 4 μm thick slice off the posterior pole contains 11.3% of total available oskar mRNA cargo in the absence of flows, only marginally less than localisation with cytoplasmic flows present.
source: A 4 μm thick slice off the posterior pole contains 11.3% of total available oskar mRNA cargo, only marginally less than localisation with cytoplasmic flows present.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation results.

claim: Cytoskeletal transport alone localises the majority of mRNA.
source: This suggests that the cytoskeletal transport alone localises the majority of mRNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing simulations with and without flows.

claim: When the motor-velocity field is set to zero or the binding constant kb is set to zero, cargo disperses throughout the oocyte without forming a central channel and completely fails to produce any posterior crescent.
source: Cargo localisation in the absence of cytoskeletal transport can be tested by either setting the motor-velocity field identical to zero vm ≡ 0, or by setting the binding constant kb to zero. In either case, cargo disperses throughout the oocyte without forming a central channel and completely fails to produce any posterior crescent.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results testing different conditions.

claim: Even under the most favourable conditions with a perfect anchor, the cytoplasmic flows cannot localise mRNA to wild-type levels.
source: Under these idealised conditions, oskar mRNA accumulates slightly at the anchor (Figure 3K). However, a 4 μm thick posterior slice contains only 2.7% of total cargo in the oocyte, about 78% less cargo than in the wild-type simulations, and only 25% more cargo compared to the purely diffusive case, which localises 2.2% of cargo. Thus, even under the most favourable conditions, the cytoplasmic flows cannot localise mRNA to wild-type levels, arguing against a mixing and entrapment mechanism for oskar mRNA localisation at stage 9.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of simulation results shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Motor-driven mRNA transport is both necessary and sufficient to account for oskar localisation.
source: Despite the small fraction of actively transported cargo (13%), motor-driven mRNA transport is both necessary and sufficient to account for oskar localisation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results testing different transport mechanisms.

claim: bicoid mRNA is believed to be transported by Dynein.
source: In contrast to oskar mRNA, bicoid mRNA is believed to be transported by Dynein (Duncan and Warrior, 2002; Januschke et al., 2002; Weil et al., 2006), but other parameters such as the fraction of bound cargo and the active transport speeds are similar to oskar mRNA (Belaya, 2008) (V Trovisco, personal communication).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Simulations show that bicoid mRNA accumulates at both posterior-lateral sides when initially placed in the posterior half of the oocyte.
source: Simulations show that bicoid mRNA accumulates at both posterior-lateral sides (Figure 3H) when initially placed in the posterior half of the oocyte (Figure 3H, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The simulated bicoid mRNA localisation is in very good agreement with experimental observations when naive bicoid mRNA is injected into the posterior region.
source: This is in very good agreement with experimental observations when naive bicoid mRNA is injected into this posterior region (Cha et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim compares simulation results with experimental observations cited from previous work.

claim: When bicoid mRNA is placed initially in the anterior-ventral region, it accumulates at the anterior and lateral cortex, in concordance with experimental observations.
source: When bicoid mRNA is placed initially in the anterior-ventral region (Figure 3I, inset), it accumulates at the anterior and lateral cortex (Figure 3I), again in concordance with the experimental observations (Cha et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim compares simulation results (Figure 3I) with experimental observations cited from previous work.

claim: Simulated localisation of bicoid mRNA remains virtually identical in the absence of cytoplasmic streaming.
source: This simulated localisation of bicoid mRNA remains virtually identical in the absence of cytoplasmic streaming.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results testing different conditions.

claim: Splitting of a bulk amount of injected bicoid mRNA occurs when the RNA is placed on the border (separatrices) between two diverging subcompartments of the MT cytoskeleton.
source: Thus, splitting of a bulk amount of injected bicoid mRNA occurs when the RNA is placed on the border (separatrices) between two diverging subcompartments of the MT cytoskeleton, each one transporting part of the cloud towards the adjacent cortex.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the simulation results based on the compartmental organization of the MT cytoskeleton.

claim: The agreement between simulations and experiments further supports an on average compartmentalised MT cytoskeleton.
source: The agreement between simulations and experiments therefore further supports an on average compartmentalised MT cytoskeleton, and naive bicoid mRNA, like oskar mRNA, unspecifically traces out the MT cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the agreement between simulation and experimental results.

claim: naive bicoid mRNA, like oskar mRNA, unspecifically traces out the MT cytoskeleton.
source: The agreement between simulations and experiments therefore further supports an on average compartmentalised MT cytoskeleton, and naive bicoid mRNA, like oskar mRNA, unspecifically traces out the MT cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results showing that both mRNAs follow the MT organization.

claim: Endogenous bicoid mRNA can be approximated by so-called conditioned bicoid mRNA that is first injected into the nurse cells, then sucked out and injected into the oocyte.
source: In contrast to naive bicoid mRNA, endogenous bicoid mRNA is transported into the oocyte after being transcribed in neighbouring nurse cells where it also becomes modified in presence of the protein Exuperantia. Endogenous bicoid mRNA can be approximated by so-called conditioned bicoid mRNA that is first injected into the nurse cells, then sucked out and injected into the oocyte.
evidence: This is a description of an experimental method based on established knowledge.

claim: Conditioned bicoid mRNA localises specifically to the anterior surface within 30 min, even if this surface is not closest to the injection site.
source: Conditioned bicoid mRNA localises specifically to the anterior surface within 30 min, even if this surface is not closest to the injection site (Cha et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: In the model, starting from an initial distribution at the anterior surface where endogenous bicoid mRNA enters the oocyte, cargo quickly moves to the anterior cortex before concentrating in the anterior corners after several hours of simulated time.
source: In the model, starting from an initial distribution at the anterior surface where endogenous bicoid mRNA enters the oocyte, cargo quickly moves to the anterior cortex before concentrating in the anterior corners after several hours of simulated time (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The simulated bicoid mRNA localisation resembles the anterior ring-like localisation of bicoid mRNA in wild-type stage 9 oocytes.
source: This resembles the anterior ring-like localisation of bicoid mRNA in wild-type stage 9 oocytes (St Johnston et al., 1989; Weil et al., 2006), and occurs independently of cytoplasmic flows.
evidence: The claim compares simulation results with experimental observations cited from previous work.

claim: The model does not reproduce transport specifically to the anterior surface when injection is further away from the anterior.
source: However, the model does not reproduce transport specifically to the anterior surface when injection is further away from the anterior.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the model based on simulation results.

claim: Exuperantia activity may enable bicoid mRNA to move along an unidentified population of MTs or allow localisation by an unknown MT-independent mechanism.
source: This suggests that Exuperantia activity somehow either enables bicoid mRNA to move along an unidentified population of MTs (Cha et al., 2001; MacDougall et al., 2003) that are not included in the computed cytoskeleton, or that it allows localisation of the mRNA by an unknown MT-independent mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms to explain the discrepancy between model and experiment, supported by citations.

claim: Cortical gradients of MT nucleation are sufficient to assemble a functional, compartmentalised MT cytoskeleton that successfully localises oskar mRNA and naive bicoid mRNA.
source: We have shown so far that cortical gradients of MT nucleation are sufficient to assemble a functional, compartmentalised MT cytoskeleton that successfully localises oskar mRNA and naive bicoid mRNA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the simulation results presented.

claim: Mutations interfering with the posterior follicle cells that surround the oocyte can disrupt the proper positioning of mRNAs.
source: Mutations interfering with the posterior follicle cells that surround the oocyte, for example, can disrupt the proper positioning of mRNAs (Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 1995; Roth et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Follicle cell clones (rasΔC40b) that are adjacent to only one side of the oocyte posterior repel cargo from that side of the cortex.
source: Specifically, follicle cell clones (rasΔC40b) that are adjacent to only one side of the oocyte posterior repel cargo from that side of the cortex (termed clone adjacent mislocalisation [Poulton and Deng, 2006]), likely due to an altered MT organisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Simulations of cargo transport with artificially added MT nucleation sites to a patch on one side of the posterior pole show that oskar mRNA is repelled from this patch and localises to the adjacent posterior boundary, in agreement with experiments.
source: To mimic this phenotype, we used an ensemble of wild-type cytoskeletons and artificially added MT nucleation sites to a patch on one side of the posterior pole. Simulations of cargo transport with diffusion, motor transport and flows show that oskar mRNA is repelled from this patch and localises to the adjacent posterior boundary, in agreement with experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and comparison with experimental observations.

claim: PAR-1 acts to suppress MT nucleation at the posterior pole of the oocyte.
source: Mislocalisation of mRNAs also occurs in mutants of the polarity protein PAR-1, which acts to suppress MT nucleation at the posterior pole of the oocyte (Shulman et al., 2000; Doerflinger et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: In strong par-1 hypomorphs with strongly reduced PAR-1 expression, MT minus ends occupy the whole cortex including the posterior pole.
source: In strong par-1 hypomorphs with strongly reduced PAR-1 expression, MT minus ends occupy the whole cortex including the posterior pole (Parton et al., 2011), thereby causing oskar mRNA to mislocalise to a dot in the centre of almost 90% of mutant oocytes (Doerflinger et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: In strong par-1 hypomorphs, oskar mRNA mislocalises to a dot in the centre of almost 90% of mutant oocytes.
source: In strong par-1 hypomorphs with strongly reduced PAR-1 expression, MT minus ends occupy the whole cortex including the posterior pole (Parton et al., 2011), thereby causing oskar mRNA to mislocalise to a dot in the centre of almost 90% of mutant oocytes (Doerflinger et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: When MT seeding points are distributed uniformly on the posterior surface in the model, the AP gradient of MT density vanishes and the directional bias of MT segments evens out.
source: To test this phenotype in the model we distributed MT seeding points uniformly on the posterior surface (Figure 4G, inset) while keeping the seeding density on the anterior surface constant. The AP gradient of MT density then vanishes and the directional bias of MT segments evens out (Figure 4G, ensemble-averaged 3D-bias: 50.1%:49.9%).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The ensemble-averaged local orientations of MTs show that MTs point towards a single focal point in the centre of the oocyte that acts as a stable fixed point of the system when MT seeding is uniform.
source: The ensemble-averaged local orientations of MTs show that MTs point towards a single focal point in the centre of the oocyte (Figure 4G) that acts as a stable fixed point of the system.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Simulations of transport with and without cytoplasmic flows show oskar mRNA concentrating in a cloud in the centre of the oocyte when MT seeding is uniform.
source: Computation of 3D flow fields for each realisation in the new ensemble (3D mean: 13.5 nm/s; 2D mean: 14.5 nm/s, N = 50) and simulations of transport with and without cytoplasmic flows show oskar mRNA concentrating in a cloud in the centre of the oocyte (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: oskar mRNA accumulation to a central dot remains unchanged if the posterior MT seeding density is decreased slightly.
source: oskar mRNA accumulation to a central dot also remains unchanged if the posterior MT seeding density is decreased slightly (Figure 4H, inset) as might be expected for hypomorphs that do not abolish PAR-1 expression completely.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Simulations of bicoid mRNA transport with slightly decreased or uniform posterior MT nucleation show the mRNA localising to the anterior corners and enriching at the posterior pole.
source: Interestingly, bicoid mRNA simulated either with slightly decreased (Figure 4H) or with uniform (Figure 4G) posterior MT nucleation not only localises to the anterior corners as in wild-type but also enriches at the posterior pole (Figure 4D, arrowheads), despite injection close to the anterior (Figure 4D, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The simulated bicoid mRNA localisation matches experiments showing bicoid mRNA mislocalisation to both anterior and posterior in gurken, torpedo and cornichon mutants.
source: This matches experiments showing bicoid mRNA mislocalisation to both anterior and posterior in gurken, torpedo and cornichon mutants (EGFR mutants) in which posterior follicle cells fail to signal a MT reorganisation in the oocyte (Gonzalez-Reyes et al., 1995; Roth et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim compares simulation results with experimental observations cited from previous work.

claim: Experiments show that bicoid mRNA localises primarily to the anterior corners and to the posterior pole in strong par-1 hypomorphs.
source: Here, using confocal fluorescence in situ hybridisation, our experiments show that bicoid mRNA localises primarily to the anterior corners and to the posterior pole in strong par-1 hypomorphs (Figure 4L), thereby mirroring EGFR mutants and agreeing with the model predictions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: (Near-)uniform MT nucleation along the posterior and lateral cortex is sufficient to explain the polarity phenotypes observed for oskar and bicoid mRNAs in gurken, torpedo and cornichon mutants and in strong par-1 hypomorphs.
source: Thus, (near-)uniform MT nucleation along the posterior and lateral cortex is sufficient to explain the polarity phenotypes observed for oskar and bicoid mRNAs in gurken, torpedo and cornichon mutants and in strong par-1 hypomorphs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the agreement between simulation and experimental results.

claim: In 10% of strong par-1 hypomorphs and 30% of weak par-1 hypomorphs, oskar mRNA is only partially mislocalised, combining a wild-type-like posterior crescent with a centrally mislocalised dot.
source: In 10% of strong par-1 hypomorphs and 30% of weak par-1 hypomorphs with weakly reduced PAR-1 expression, oskar mRNA is only partially mislocalised, combining a wild-type-like posterior crescent with a centrally mislocalised dot (Doerflinger et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Increasing MT nucleation laterally towards the posterior pole creates a stable focus in the centre of the oocyte whose domain of attraction does not cover the entire oocyte, with a small basin of attraction towards the posterior pole persisting.
source: Increasing MT nucleation laterally towards the posterior pole (Figure 4G, inset) again creates a stable focus in the centre of the oocyte. However, its domain of attraction does not cover the entire oocyte. Instead, a small basin of attraction towards the posterior pole persists (Figure 4G, red), separated from the basin of attraction of the stable focus by an unstable saddle-node point.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Cargo simulated on cytoskeletons with stable and unstable fixed points can split into two separate accumulations, first at the posterior pole and second in a dot along the AP-axis.
source: Cargo simulated on cytoskeletons with stable and unstable fixed points and their corresponding flow fields can split into two separate accumulations, first at the posterior pole and second in a dot along the AP-axis (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The agreement between simulations and experimental results suggests that intermediate levels of PAR-1 at the posterior lead to a cytoskeleton with a potential barrier between the oocyte centre and its posterior pole.
source: This agreement with experimental results suggests that intermediate levels of PAR-1 at the posterior lead to a cytoskeleton with a potential barrier between the oocyte centre and its posterior pole.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the agreement between simulation and experimental results.

claim: Modulation of MT nucleation along the posterior-lateral cortex alone is sufficient to capture the partial mislocalisation phenotype.
source: It also shows that modulation of MT nucleation along the posterior-lateral cortex alone is sufficient to capture this.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Diffusion and flows can aid posterior localisation by pushing unbound cargo across the unstable point and increasing the amount of oskar mRNA that reaches the posterior pole.
source: Because the potential barrier only affects the bound state, diffusion and flows can aid posterior localisation in this context by pushing unbound cargo across the unstable point and increasing the amount of oskar mRNA that reaches the posterior pole.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism based on the simulation results.

claim: Variations of MT nucleation along the cortex can account for the mislocalisations of bicoid and oskar mRNAs in polarity mutants.
source: In summary, variations of MT nucleation along the cortex not only explain mRNA localisations in wild-type but can also account for the mislocalisations of bicoid and oskar mRNAs in polarity mutants.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the simulation results for different mutant conditions.

claim: The creation of stable and unstable fixed points in the transition from wild-type to strong par-1 hypomorph topology constitutes a classical saddle-node bifurcation.
source: The creation of stable and unstable fixed points in the transition from wild-type to strong par-1 hypomorph topology constitutes a classical saddle-node bifurcation (Figure 4K–M, 'Materials and methods' Bifurcation normal form) with the cortical MT seeding density as the bifurcation parameter.
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical analysis shown in Figure 4K-M and described in the methods.

claim: In both the polymer model and the rod model, the mean length of MTs acts as a second bifurcation parameter.
source: Interestingly, in both the polymer model and the rod model, the mean length of MTs acts as a second bifurcation parameter.
evidence: This is a statement about the model behavior based on computational analysis.

claim: For sufficiently short MT filaments, few MTs from the anterior can reach and contribute to orientations in the posterior half of the oocyte.
source: For example, for sufficiently short MT filaments (Figure 4K), few MTs from the anterior can reach and contribute to orientations in the posterior half of the oocyte.
